claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) integrates incoming information to guide actions.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) integrates incoming information to guide our actions.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on PFC function.

claim: Platform-mediated active avoidance requires prelimbic (PL) PFC.
source: This avoidance requires prelimbic (PL) PFC, basolateral amygdala (BLA), and ventral striatum (VS).
evidence: Stated as a requirement based on prior research.

claim: Platform-mediated active avoidance requires basolateral amygdala (BLA).
source: This avoidance requires prelimbic (PL) PFC, basolateral amygdala (BLA), and ventral striatum (VS).
evidence: Stated as a requirement based on prior research.

claim: Platform-mediated active avoidance requires ventral striatum (VS).
source: This avoidance requires prelimbic (PL) PFC, basolateral amygdala (BLA), and ventral striatum (VS).
evidence: Stated as a requirement based on prior research.

claim: Inhibitory tone responses of PL neurons correlate with avoidability of shock.
source: We previously showed that inhibitory tone responses of PL neurons correlate with avoidability of shock (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study by the authors.

claim: Photoactivating PL-VS projections reduced avoidance.
source: Photoactivating PL-VS projections reduced avoidance, whereas photoactivating PL-BLA projections increased avoidance.
evidence: Experimental finding from optogenetic manipulation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Photoactivating PL-BLA projections increased avoidance.
source: Photoactivating PL-VS projections reduced avoidance, whereas photoactivating PL-BLA projections increased avoidance.
evidence: Experimental finding from optogenetic manipulation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Photosilencing PL-BLA projections reduced avoidance.
source: Moreover, photosilencing PL-BLA or BLA-VS projections reduced avoidance, suggesting that VS receives opposing inputs from PL and BLA.
evidence: Experimental finding from optogenetic manipulation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Photosilencing BLA-VS projections reduced avoidance.
source: Moreover, photosilencing PL-BLA or BLA-VS projections reduced avoidance, suggesting that VS receives opposing inputs from PL and BLA.
evidence: Experimental finding from optogenetic manipulation reported in the manuscript.

claim: VS receives opposing inputs from PL and BLA.
source: Moreover, photosilencing PL-BLA or BLA-VS projections reduced avoidance, suggesting that VS receives opposing inputs from PL and BLA.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results of photosilencing experiments.

claim: Bidirectional modulation of avoidance by PL projections to VS and BLA enables the animal to make appropriate decisions when faced with competing drives.
source: Bidirectional modulation of avoidance by PL projections to VS and BLA enables the animal to make appropriate decisions when faced with competing drives.
evidence: Interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The PFC evaluates possible outcomes in the presence of competing drives.
source: A leading hypothesis is that the PFC evaluates possible outcomes in the presence of competing drives (Ridderinkhof et al., 2004; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Bissonette et al., 2013; Saunders et al., 2017), such as seeking food rewards in the presence of a potential threat (Aupperle et al., 2015; Friedman et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 2016; Bublatzky et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Activity in the prelimbic (PL) PFC is necessary for the expression of PMA.
source: Activity in the prelimbic (PL) PFC is necessary for the expression of PMA (Bravo-Rivera et al., 2014; Diehl et al., 2018), but little is known about the circuit-level mechanisms of the PFC that control this type of avoidance.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Neurons in PL show both excitatory and inhibitory responses to the tone during PMA.
source: During PMA, neurons in PL show both excitatory and inhibitory responses to the tone (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Similar excitatory tone responses in PL are observed in fear-conditioned rats.
source: Similar excitatory tone responses in PL are observed in fear-conditioned rats (Burgos-Robles et al., 2009), but inhibitory tone responses are limited to rats trained in PMA, suggesting the existence of a disinhibitory PL circuit for expression of avoidance (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Inhibitory tone responses are limited to rats trained in PMA.
source: Similar excitatory tone responses in PL are observed in fear-conditioned rats (Burgos-Robles et al., 2009), but inhibitory tone responses are limited to rats trained in PMA, suggesting the existence of a disinhibitory PL circuit for expression of avoidance (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: There exists a disinhibitory PL circuit for expression of avoidance.
source: Similar excitatory tone responses in PL are observed in fear-conditioned rats (Burgos-Robles et al., 2009), but inhibitory tone responses are limited to rats trained in PMA, suggesting the existence of a disinhibitory PL circuit for expression of avoidance (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on the observation of inhibitory responses specific to PMA.

claim: PL projects heavily to the ventral striatum (VS).
source: PL projects heavily to the ventral striatum (VS) and the basolateral amygdala (BLA) (Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2004), both of which are necessary for PMA (Bravo-Rivera et al., 2014) as well as other types of active avoidance (Darvas et al., 2011; Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: PL projects heavily to the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
source: PL projects heavily to the ventral striatum (VS) and the basolateral amygdala (BLA) (Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2004), both of which are necessary for PMA (Bravo-Rivera et al., 2014) as well as other types of active avoidance (Darvas et al., 2011; Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: VS and BLA are necessary for PMA.
source: PL projects heavily to the ventral striatum (VS) and the basolateral amygdala (BLA) (Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2004), both of which are necessary for PMA (Bravo-Rivera et al., 2014) as well as other types of active avoidance (Darvas et al., 2011; Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: VS and BLA are necessary for other types of active avoidance.
source: PL projects heavily to the ventral striatum (VS) and the basolateral amygdala (BLA) (Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2004), both of which are necessary for PMA (Bravo-Rivera et al., 2014) as well as other types of active avoidance (Darvas et al., 2011; Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Inhibitory responses in PL neurons projecting to the VS would promote avoidance.
source: Because PL projects densely to the VS (Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2004), we hypothesized that inhibitory responses in PL neurons projecting to the VS would promote avoidance.
evidence: Hypothesis stated by the authors based on anatomical projections.

claim: Activating PL neurons projecting to VS with channelrhodopsin (ChR2) would be expected to impair avoidance.
source: If so, activating these projection neurons with channelrhodopsin (ChR2) would be expected to impair avoidance.
evidence: Prediction based on the hypothesis about inhibitory responses.

claim: Expression of ChR2 was largely confined to rostral PL with some spread to rostral anterior cingulate (Cg1) and caudal PL.
source: Histological analysis showed that expression of ChR2 was largely confined to rostral PL with some spread to rostral anterior cingulate (Cg1) and caudal PL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Histological data presented in the manuscript and referenced figure.

claim: ChR2 photoactivation at 4 Hz significantly reduced the time spent on the platform during the tone, compared to eYFP controls.
source: Figure 1C shows that ChR2 photoactivation at either frequency significantly reduced the time spent on the platform during the tone, compared to eYFP controls (4 Hz: eYFP 77% vs. ChR2 51%, t(18)=2.370, p>0.05, Bonferroni corrected; 15 Hz: eYFP 88% vs. ChR2 22%, t(18)=7.152, p<0.01, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ChR2 photoactivation at 15 Hz significantly reduced the time spent on the platform during the tone, compared to eYFP controls.
source: Figure 1C shows that ChR2 photoactivation at either frequency significantly reduced the time spent on the platform during the tone, compared to eYFP controls (4 Hz: eYFP 77% vs. ChR2 51%, t(18)=2.370, p>0.05, Bonferroni corrected; 15 Hz: eYFP 88% vs. ChR2 22%, t(18)=7.152, p<0.01, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ChR2 rats were significantly delayed in their avoidance 3–6 s after tone onset during 4 Hz photoactivation.
source: Analysis of avoidance across the tone in 3 s bins (Figure 1D) indicated that ChR2 rats were significantly delayed in their avoidance 3–6 s after tone onset during 4 Hz photoactivation (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,9) = 5.88, p=0.026; post-hoc Tukey test, 3–6 s p=0.029).
evidence: Statistical analysis of time-course data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Photoactivation at 15 Hz had a stronger effect, with ChR2 rats showing a significant reduction of avoidance throughout the tone.
source: Photoactivation at 15 Hz had a stronger effect, with ChR2 rats showing a significant reduction of avoidance throughout the tone (Figure 1E, repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,9) = 48.92, p<0.001; post-hoc Tukey test, 6–30 s, all p's < 0.01).
evidence: Statistical analysis of time-course data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Photoactivation of PL-VS projections had no effect on locomotion.
source: Photoactivation of PL-VS projections had no effect on locomotion, as indicated by distance traveled in an open field (4 Hz; eYFP n = 15, 2.7 m vs. ChR2 n = 7, 2.2 m, t(20)=1.54 p=0.138), nor on anxiety levels, as both groups spent a similar amount of time in the center of the open field (4 Hz: eYFP n = 15, 4.1 s vs. ChR2 n = 7, 6.4 s, t(20)=1.17, p=0.255).
evidence: Statistical analysis of open field test data.

claim: Photoactivation of PL-VS projections had no effect on anxiety levels.
source: Photoactivation of PL-VS projections had no effect on locomotion, as indicated by distance traveled in an open field (4 Hz; eYFP n = 15, 2.7 m vs. ChR2 n = 7, 2.2 m, t(20)=1.54 p=0.138), nor on anxiety levels, as both groups spent a similar amount of time in the center of the open field (4 Hz: eYFP n = 15, 4.1 s vs. ChR2 n = 7, 6.4 s, t(20)=1.17, p=0.255).
evidence: Statistical analysis of open field test data.

claim: Photoactivation of PL terminals in VS during the tone impaired the expression of avoidance, similar to photoactivation of PL somata.
source: Thus, photoactivation of PL terminals in VS during the tone impaired the expression of avoidance, similar to photoactivation of PL somata (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison of current findings with prior study results.

claim: Photosilencing PL-VS projections would enhance avoidance.
source: If photoactivation impairs avoidance, we hypothesized that photosilencing PL-VS projections would enhance avoidance, similar to what we observed when photosilencing PL somata (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Hypothesis stated by the authors based on prior findings.

claim: Photosilencing PL-VS projections had no significant effect on average avoidance levels.
source: However, photosilencing PL-VS projections had no significant effect on average avoidance levels (Figure 1G, eYFP 76% vs. ArchT 69%, t(20)=0.8498, p=0.406) or on the timecourse of avoidance across the tone (Figure 1H, repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,9)=0.7088, p=0.410).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: Photosilencing PL-VS projections had no effect on spontaneous bar-pressing.
source: Photosilencing PL-VS projections also had no effect on spontaneous bar-pressing (ArchT, n = 9, seven average number of presses during laser OFF vs. six average number of presses during laser ON, t(8)=1.32, p=0.224).
evidence: Statistical analysis of bar-pressing data.

claim: PL excitation was not necessary for avoidance, because photosilencing PL somata did not impair avoidance.
source: Our previous study suggested that PL excitation was not necessary for avoidance, because photosilencing PL somata did not impair avoidance (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of prior study results.

claim: Excitatory responses of PL neurons were observed during both tone onset and platform entry.
source: Nevertheless, excitatory responses of PL neurons were observed during both tone onset and platform entry, and the opposing effects on behavior of inhibitory and excitatory responses may have been masked by our non-specific targeting of PL somata.
evidence: Observation from prior study and inference about masking effects.

claim: PL sends strong projections to BLA.
source: Anatomical studies demonstrate strong projections from PL to BLA (Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: PL-BLA photoactivation at 4 Hz did not significantly affect avoidance.
source: In contrast to PL-VS photoactivation, PL-BLA photoactivation at 4 or 15 Hz did not impair avoidance; in fact, avoidance significantly increased with 15 Hz photoactivation (Figures 2B, 4 Hz: eYFP 80% vs. ChR2 90%, t(11)=1.652, p=0.127; 15 Hz: eYFP 75% vs. ChR2 88%, t(15)=2.700, p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Avoidance significantly increased with 15 Hz photoactivation of PL-BLA projections.
source: In contrast to PL-VS photoactivation, PL-BLA photoactivation at 4 or 15 Hz did not impair avoidance; in fact, avoidance significantly increased with 15 Hz photoactivation (Figures 2B, 4 Hz: eYFP 80% vs. ChR2 90%, t(11)=1.652, p=0.127; 15 Hz: eYFP 75% vs. ChR2 88%, t(15)=2.700, p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 15 Hz photoactivation of PL-BLA projections increased avoidance at both 3 s and 6 s time bins.
source: Analysis across the tone (Figure 2C–D) revealed increased avoidance with 15 Hz photoactivation at both 3 s and 6 s time bins (Mann-Whitney U-test, 3–6 s p=0.006, 6–9 s p=0.027).
evidence: Statistical analysis of time-course data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: The small effect of photoactivation of PL-BLA projections is likely due to ceiling levels of avoidance.
source: The small effect of photoactivation of PL-BLA projections is likely due to ceiling levels of avoidance, as control rats avoided at 82% (Figure 2B, No Laser Cond).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results based on observed baseline avoidance levels.

claim: Photoactivation of PL terminals in BLA (at 15 Hz) significantly increased avoidance compared to eYFP controls after extinction.
source: On the last trial of extinction, photoactivation of PL terminals in BLA (at 15 Hz) significantly increased avoidance compared to eYFP controls (eYFP 2.4% vs. ChR2 34.5% time on platform, t(6)=3.269, p=0.017).
evidence: Statistical analysis of extinction reinstatement data.

claim: Photoactivation of PL-BLA pathway did not affect locomotion.
source: Photoactivation of this pathway did not affect locomotion (15 Hz: n = 6 eYFP, 3.2 m vs. n = 5 ChR2, 3.1 m of distance traveled in an open field, t(9)=0.196, p=0.849), or anxiety levels (15 Hz: n = 6 eYFP, 5.1 s vs. n = 5 ChR2, 4.0 s of time spent in center of open field, t(9)=0.318, p=0.757;).
evidence: Statistical analysis of open field test data.

claim: Photoactivation of PL-BLA pathway did not affect anxiety levels.
source: Photoactivation of this pathway did not affect locomotion (15 Hz: n = 6 eYFP, 3.2 m vs. n = 5 ChR2, 3.1 m of distance traveled in an open field, t(9)=0.196, p=0.849), or anxiety levels (15 Hz: n = 6 eYFP, 5.1 s vs. n = 5 ChR2, 4.0 s of time spent in center of open field, t(9)=0.318, p=0.757;).
evidence: Statistical analysis of open field test data.

claim: PL activation of BLA promotes avoidance.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that PL activation of BLA promotes avoidance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: Photosilencing PL-BLA projections significantly impaired the expression of avoidance.
source: Photosilencing PL-BLA projections significantly impaired the expression of avoidance (Figure 2G, eYFP 77% vs. ArchT 38% time on platform, t(18)=2.985, p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ArchT rats showed an overall decrease in avoidance across the tone compared to eYFP controls when PL-BLA projections were photosilenced.
source: Furthermore, ArchT rats showed an overall decrease in avoidance across the tone compared to eYFP controls (Figure 2H, repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,9)=9.449, p=0.007, post-hoc Tukey tests, 3–9 and 12–24 s, all p's < 0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of time-course data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Photosilencing PL-BLA projections had no effect on spontaneous bar-pressing.
source: Photosilencing PL-BLA projections had no effect on spontaneous bar-pressing (ArchT n = 11, 4.82 average number of presses during laser OFF vs. 5.77 average number of presses during laser ON, p=0.255, t(10)=1.21).
evidence: Statistical analysis of bar-pressing data.

claim: PL excitation of BLA is necessary for the expression of active avoidance.
source: These findings suggest that PL excitation of BLA is necessary for the expression of active avoidance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the photosilencing experiments.

claim: Distinct PL projections have opposite roles in avoidance: PL-VS projections inhibit avoidance whereas PL-BLA projections promote avoidance.
source: Thus far, distinct PL projections appear to have opposite roles in avoidance: PL-VS projections inhibit avoidance whereas PL-BLA projections promote avoidance.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from PL-VS and PL-BLA manipulations.

claim: BLA sends strong projections to VS.
source: Previous studies have shown that BLA sends strong projections to VS (Kelley et al., 1982; Mcdonald, 1991a; Mcdonald, 1991b), and pharmacological disconnection of BLA and VS impairs shuttle avoidance (Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Pharmacological disconnection of BLA and VS impairs shuttle avoidance.
source: Previous studies have shown that BLA sends strong projections to VS (Kelley et al., 1982; Mcdonald, 1991a; Mcdonald, 1991b), and pharmacological disconnection of BLA and VS impairs shuttle avoidance (Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: BLA-VS projections may promote avoidance.
source: Therefore, we reasoned that BLA-VS projections may also promote avoidance.
evidence: Hypothesis based on anatomical and functional evidence.

claim: Photoactivation of BLA-VS projections at 4 Hz did not significantly increase avoidance.
source: Following ChR2 infusion into BLA and implantation of optic fibers targeting the VS (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), photoactivation of BLA-VS projections slightly increased avoidance, but this did not reach statistical significance (Figure 3B) at 4 Hz (eYFP 70% vs. ChR2 90% time on platform, t(12)=1.678, p=0.119) or 15 Hz (eYFP 70% vs ChR2 86% time on platform, t(12)=1.50, p=0.159).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Photoactivation of BLA-VS projections at 15 Hz did not significantly increase avoidance.
source: Following ChR2 infusion into BLA and implantation of optic fibers targeting the VS (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), photoactivation of BLA-VS projections slightly increased avoidance, but this did not reach statistical significance (Figure 3B) at 4 Hz (eYFP 70% vs. ChR2 90% time on platform, t(12)=1.678, p=0.119) or 15 Hz (eYFP 70% vs ChR2 86% time on platform, t(12)=1.50, p=0.159).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A ceiling effect was observed during photoactivation of BLA-VS projections.
source: Similar to photoactivation of PL-BLA projections, a ceiling effect was observed during photoactivation of BLA-VS projections.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results based on high baseline avoidance.

claim: Photoactivation of BLA-VS projections at 15 Hz significantly increased avoidance expression after extinction.
source: In the final trial of extinction training, photoactivation of BLA-VS projections at 15 Hz significantly increased avoidance expression (eYFP 9% vs. ChR2 38% time on platform, t(11)=3.521, p=0.005).
evidence: Statistical analysis of extinction reinstatement data.

claim: Photoactivation of BLA-VS projections did not affect locomotion.
source: Photoactivation did not affect locomotion (15 Hz: n = 5 eYFP, 2.7 m vs. n = 7 ChR2, 3.2 m of distance traveled in an open field, t(10)=1.10, p=0.298), or anxiety levels (15 Hz: n = 5 eYFP, 4.0 s vs. n = 7 ChR2, 4.2 s of time spent in center of open field, t(10)=0.0085, p=0.934).
evidence: Statistical analysis of open field test data.

claim: Photoactivation of BLA-VS projections did not affect anxiety levels.
source: Photoactivation did not affect locomotion (15 Hz: n = 5 eYFP, 2.7 m vs. n = 7 ChR2, 3.2 m of distance traveled in an open field, t(10)=1.10, p=0.298), or anxiety levels (15 Hz: n = 5 eYFP, 4.0 s vs. n = 7 ChR2, 4.2 s of time spent in center of open field, t(10)=0.0085, p=0.934).
evidence: Statistical analysis of open field test data.

claim: BLA-VS projections facilitate the expression of avoidance.
source: Taken together, these findings show that BLA-VS projections facilitate the expression of avoidance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the photoactivation experiments.

claim: Photosilencing BLA-VS projections significantly impaired the expression of avoidance.
source: Photosilencing BLA-VS projections significantly impaired the expression of avoidance (Figure 3G, eYFP 78% vs. ArchT 28%, t(19)=3.849, p<0.01, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: ArchT rats showed a decrease in avoidance throughout the tone when BLA-VS projections were photosilenced, compared to eYFP controls.
source: Furthermore, ArchT rats showed a decrease in avoidance throughout the tone, compared to eYFP controls (Figure 3H, repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,9)=5.23, p=0.034, post-hoc Tukey tests, 6–15 s, all p's < 0.01, 15–18 s, p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of time-course data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Photosilencing BLA-VS projections did not affect spontaneous bar-pressing.
source: Photosilencing BLA-VS projections did not affect spontaneous bar-pressing (ArchT n = 6, 5.75 average number of presses during laser OFF vs. 7.58 average number of presses during laser ON, t(5)=1.27, p=0.259).
evidence: Statistical analysis of bar-pressing data.

claim: BLA excitation of VS is necessary for the expression of active avoidance.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that BLA excitation of VS is necessary for the expression of active avoidance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the photosilencing experiments.

claim: Photoactivation of PL-VS projections impaired avoidance.
source: We found that photoactivation of PL-VS projections impaired avoidance, whereas photoactivation of PL-BLA projections promoted avoidance, suggesting a prefrontal circuit that bidirectionally modulates avoidance behavior.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings.

claim: Photoactivation of PL-BLA projections promoted avoidance.
source: We found that photoactivation of PL-VS projections impaired avoidance, whereas photoactivation of PL-BLA projections promoted avoidance, suggesting a prefrontal circuit that bidirectionally modulates avoidance behavior.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings.

claim: There exists a prefrontal circuit that bidirectionally modulates avoidance behavior.
source: We found that photoactivation of PL-VS projections impaired avoidance, whereas photoactivation of PL-BLA projections promoted avoidance, suggesting a prefrontal circuit that bidirectionally modulates avoidance behavior.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: VS receives excitation from the BLA to promote avoidance.
source: Optogenetic manipulations of BLA-VS projections also revealed that VS receives excitation from the BLA to promote avoidance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the BLA-VS manipulation experiments.

claim: A ceiling effect prevented observation of an increase in avoidance when PL-VS projections were photosilenced.
source: One possibility is that a ceiling effect prevented us from observing an increase in avoidance, as we had observed in our initial study when PL somata were photosilenced (see Figure 2E in Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation about why photosilencing PL-VS did not enhance avoidance.

claim: Some of the optic probes for ArchT PL-VS experiments ended up targeting the shell rather than the core of the VS.
source: A second possibility is that some of the optic probes for our ArchT PL-VS experiments ended up targeting the shell rather than the core of the VS (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), possibly suppressing any effect of our PL-VS manipulation.
evidence: Speculation based on histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The PL-VS projection targets the core region of the VS.
source: Anatomical studies show that the PL-VS projection targets the core region of the VS, whereas PL-BLA projection targets the shell region of the VS (Heimer et al., 1997; Gorelova and Yang, 1996; Zahm, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The PL-BLA projection targets the shell region of the VS.
source: Anatomical studies show that the PL-VS projection targets the core region of the VS, whereas PL-BLA projection targets the shell region of the VS (Heimer et al., 1997; Gorelova and Yang, 1996; Zahm, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Photosilencing PL-VS fibers may have inadvertently photosilenced fibers of passage from PL to BLA.
source: Thus, photosilencing PL-VS fibers with the approach we used may have inadvertently photosilenced fibers of passage from PL to BLA, which could cancel out facilitating effects, as photosilencing PL-BLA decreases avoidance.
evidence: Speculation about potential confound in the photosilencing experiments.

claim: Photoactivating PL-VS projections impaired avoidance, in agreement with previous findings that photoactivation of PL somata impaired avoidance.
source: Despite the lack of effect of photosilencing PL-VS projections, we did observe that photoactivating PL-VS projections impaired avoidance. This is in agreement with our previous findings that photoactivation of PL somata impaired avoidance (Diehl et al., 2018), and provides indirect evidence that PL inhibition facilitates avoidance.
evidence: Comparison of current findings with prior study results.

claim: PL inhibition facilitates avoidance.
source: Despite the lack of effect of photosilencing PL-VS projections, we did observe that photoactivating PL-VS projections impaired avoidance. This is in agreement with our previous findings that photoactivation of PL somata impaired avoidance (Diehl et al., 2018), and provides indirect evidence that PL inhibition facilitates avoidance.
evidence: Inference drawn from the photoactivation results.

claim: The inhibitory tone response in PL targets the VS to drive avoidance.
source: This suggests that the inhibitory tone response in PL targets the VS to drive avoidance.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Excitatory projections from PL to BLA drive avoidance.
source: In contrast, we found that excitatory projections from PL to BLA drive avoidance (see model in Figure 4).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: PL neurons showing inhibitory tone responses project to VS.
source: Future studies using PMA could determine if PL neurons showing inhibitory tone responses project to VS, and if PL neurons showing excitatory responses project to BLA by employing photoexcitation-assisted identification of neuronal populations (Jennings et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Ciocchi et al., 2015; Beyeler et al., 2016; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation about future experiments to test this hypothesis.

claim: PL neurons showing excitatory responses project to BLA.
source: Future studies using PMA could determine if PL neurons showing inhibitory tone responses project to VS, and if PL neurons showing excitatory responses project to BLA by employing photoexcitation-assisted identification of neuronal populations (Jennings et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Ciocchi et al., 2015; Beyeler et al., 2016; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation about future experiments to test this hypothesis.

claim: PL-VS projections promote reward-seeking.
source: PL-VS projections were shown to promote reward-seeking, whereas PL-thalamic projections inhibited reward-seeking (Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: PL-thalamic projections inhibited reward-seeking.
source: PL-VS projections were shown to promote reward-seeking, whereas PL-thalamic projections inhibited reward-seeking (Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: PL dopamine (D2) neurons targeting the BLA signaled the probability of receiving a reward.
source: A study of decision making demonstrated that PL dopamine (D2) neurons targeting the BLA signaled the probability of receiving a reward, whereas PL dopamine (D1) neurons targeting the VS signaled the probability of reward omission (Jenni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: PL dopamine (D1) neurons targeting the VS signaled the probability of reward omission.
source: A study of decision making demonstrated that PL dopamine (D2) neurons targeting the BLA signaled the probability of receiving a reward, whereas PL dopamine (D1) neurons targeting the VS signaled the probability of reward omission (Jenni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: OFC-VS projections were necessary for using negative outcomes to guide choices.
source: Additionally, a probabilistic reversal learning task investigating the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) found that OFC-VS projections were necessary for using negative outcomes to guide choices, whereas OFC-amygdala projections were necessary for stabilizing the value of actions (Groman et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: OFC-amygdala projections were necessary for stabilizing the value of actions.
source: Additionally, a probabilistic reversal learning task investigating the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) found that OFC-VS projections were necessary for using negative outcomes to guide choices, whereas OFC-amygdala projections were necessary for stabilizing the value of actions (Groman et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Bidirectional control of behavior can be governed by specific circuits within PFC, allowing for the selection of the appropriate behavioral response.
source: Collectively, these studies demonstrate that bidirectional control of behavior can be governed by specific circuits within PFC, allowing for the selection of the appropriate behavioral response.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple cited studies.

claim: Pre-training lesions in VS enhance avoidance responses in shuttle-box avoidance task.
source: A previous study using the shuttle-box avoidance task reported that pre-training lesions in VS enhance avoidance responses (Lichtenberg et al., 2014), which disagrees with the current study.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Other structures may compensate for the loss of VS after lesions.
source: However, successful avoidance was measured on the 7th day of training after lesions were made, introducing the possibility that other structures compensated for the loss of VS (Anglada-Figueroa and Quirk, 2005), thereby forcing an alternative circuit to acquire the task.
evidence: Speculation about potential confound in prior study, supported by citation.

claim: Disconnecting BLA from VS impaired avoidance in shuttle-box avoidance.
source: Another shuttle-box avoidance study showed that disconnecting BLA from VS impaired avoidance (Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The activity of BLA terminals within VS is necessary for avoidance.
source: Our findings extend this by showing that the activity of BLA terminals within VS is necessary for avoidance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the current experimental findings.

claim: A subset of BLA neurons projecting to VS receive inputs from PL.
source: A subset of BLA neurons projecting to VS have been shown to receive inputs from PL (McGarry and Carter, 2017), consistent with our model (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study and consistent with the model in Figure 4.

claim: PL bidirectionally controls active avoidance by modulating the effect of BLA inputs to VS.
source: Here, we propose that PL bidirectionally controls active avoidance by modulating the effect of BLA inputs to VS, through activation of BLA and/or feed-forward inhibition of VS, perhaps via fast-spiking interneurons (Berke, 2011).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: PL may modulate VS through feed-forward inhibition via fast-spiking interneurons.
source: Here, we propose that PL bidirectionally controls active avoidance by modulating the effect of BLA inputs to VS, through activation of BLA and/or feed-forward inhibition of VS, perhaps via fast-spiking interneurons (Berke, 2011).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: PL driving of avoidance may be most pronounced during the early part of the tone in PMA.
source: In PMA, PL driving of avoidance may be most pronounced during the early part of the tone, as pharmacological inactivation of PL delays but does not prevent avoidance (Diehl et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference based on prior pharmacological inactivation study.

claim: BLA projections to VS may override feed-forward inhibition from PL to VS as the tone progresses.
source: This suggests that BLA projections to VS may override feed-forward inhibition from PL to VS, as the tone progresses and there is increased urgency to avoid.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental findings and temporal dynamics of avoidance.

claim: The rodent PL is thought to be homologous to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) in humans.
source: The rodent PL is thought to be homologous to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) in humans (Bicks et al., 2015; Heilbronner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative neuroanatomy studies.

claim: Decreased activity in dACC correlates with the predictability of an aversive stimulus.
source: Neuroimaging studies have found that decreased activity in dACC correlates with the predictability of an aversive stimulus (Wood et al., 2015) and the avoidance of a threat (Aupperle et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Decreased activation of dACC during threat avoidance was accompanied by increased activation of VS.
source: In the latter case, decreased activation of dACC was accompanied by increased activation of VS.
evidence: Supported by citation to neuroimaging study.

claim: Increased coupling between dACC and amygdala occurs during active avoidance.
source: Another study showed increased coupling between dACC and amygdala during active avoidance (Collins et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to neuroimaging study.

claim: Human neuroimaging findings demonstrate bidirectional control of active avoidance by dACC.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate bidirectional control of active avoidance by dACC and are consistent with PL in rodents guiding appropriate action during the tone (lever pressing vs. moving to the platform).
evidence: Inference drawn from multiple cited neuroimaging studies.

claim: PL in rodents guides appropriate action during the tone (lever pressing vs. moving to the platform).
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate bidirectional control of active avoidance by dACC and are consistent with PL in rodents guiding appropriate action during the tone (lever pressing vs. moving to the platform).
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental findings and comparison with human studies.

claim: 118 adult male Sprague Dawley rats aged 3–5 months and weighing 320–420 g were used in the study.
source: 118 adult male Sprague Dawley rats (Envigo Laboratories, Indianapolis, IN) aged 3–5 months and weighing 320–420 g were housed and handled as previously described (Diehl et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of experimental subjects.

claim: Rats were kept on a restricted diet (18 g/day) of standard laboratory rat chow.
source: Rats were kept on a restricted diet (18 g/day) of standard laboratory rat chow to facilitate pressing a bar for sucrose pellets (BioServ, Flemington, NJ) on a variable interval schedule of reinforcement (VI-30).
evidence: Description of experimental methods.

claim: Rats were trained until they reached a criterion of >15 presses/min.
source: Rats were trained until they reached a criterion of >15 presses/min.
evidence: Description of training criterion.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Puerto Rico School of Medicine.
source: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Puerto Rico School of Medicine in compliance with the National Institutes of Health guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: Viral vectors were bilaterally infused in the PL PFC at coordinates +3.15 mm AP; ±0.40 mm ML; −3.60 mm DV to bregma, at a 0° angle.
source: For optogenetic experiments, rats were bilaterally infused with viral vectors in the PL PFC(+3.15 mm AP;±0.40 mm ML; −3.60 mm DV to bregma, at a 0°angle) or the BLA ( −2.8 mm AP,±4.8 mm ML, −8.9 mm DV).
evidence: Description of surgical methods.

claim: Viral vectors were bilaterally infused in the BLA at coordinates −2.8 mm AP, ±4.8 mm ML, −8.9 mm DV.
source: For optogenetic experiments, rats were bilaterally infused with viral vectors in the PL PFC(+3.15 mm AP;±0.40 mm ML; −3.60 mm DV to bregma, at a 0°angle) or the BLA ( −2.8 mm AP,±4.8 mm ML, −8.9 mm DV).
evidence: Description of surgical methods.

claim: Optical fibers were chronically implanted for PL or BLA terminal illumination.
source: Optical fibers (length, 9 mm; 0.22 NA; 200 nm core; constructed with products from Thorlabs, Newton, NJ or purchased preassembled from Newdoon, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China) were chronically implanted for PL or BLA terminal illumination.
evidence: Description of surgical methods.

claim: For PL terminals, fibers were placed in the VS at coordinates +1.2 mm AP, ±3.0 mm ML, −3.6 mm DV, at a 15° angle.
source: For PL terminals, fibers were placed in the VS (+1.2 mm AP,±3.0 mm ML, −3.6 mm DV, at a 15° angle) or the BLA (−2.8 mm AP,±4.8 mm ML, −7.7 mm DV, at a 0°angle).
evidence: Description of surgical methods.

claim: For PL terminals, fibers were placed in the BLA at coordinates −2.8 mm AP, ±4.8 mm ML, −7.7 mm DV, at a 0° angle.
source: For PL terminals, fibers were placed in the VS (+1.2 mm AP,±3.0 mm ML, −3.6 mm DV, at a 15° angle) or the BLA (−2.8 mm AP,±4.8 mm ML, −7.7 mm DV, at a 0°angle).
evidence: Description of surgical methods.

claim: For BLA terminals, fibers were placed in the VS at coordinates +1.0 mm AP, ±3.0 mm ML, −6.5 mm DV, at a 15° angle.
source: For BLA terminals, fibers were placed in the VS (+1.0 mm AP,±3.0 mm ML, −6.5 mm DV, at a 15°angle).
evidence: Description of surgical methods.

claim: Rats were allowed a minimum of 7 days to recover from surgery prior to behavioral training.
source: Rats were allowed a minimum of 7 days to recover from surgery prior to behavioral training.
evidence: Description of experimental timeline.

claim: Rats expressing ChR2 in PL or BLA were illuminated using a blue diode-pump solid state laser (DPSS, 473 nm, 4 or 15 Hz, 5 ms pulse width, 8–12 mW at the optical fiber tip).
source: Rats expressing channelrhodopsin (ChR2) in PL or BLA were illuminated using a blue diode-pump solid state laser (DPSS, 473 nm, 4 or 15 Hz, 5 ms pulse width, 8–12 mW at the optical fiber tip; OptoEngine, Midvale, UT), similar to our previous study (Do-Monte et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of optogenetic methods.

claim: Rats expressing ArchT in PL were bilaterally illuminated using a DPSS green laser (532 nm, constant, 12–15 mW at the optical fiber tip).
source: Rats expressing archaerhodopsin (ArchT) in PL were bilaterally illuminated using a DPSS green laser (532 nm, constant, 12–15 mW at the optical fiber tip; OptoEngine).
evidence: Description of optogenetic methods.

claim: The laser was activated at tone onset and persisted throughout the 30 s tone presentation.
source: For both ChR2 and ArchT experiments, the laser was activated at tone onset and persisted throughout the 30 s tone presentation.
evidence: Description of optogenetic stimulation protocol.

claim: The CaMKIIα promoter enables transgene expression favoring pyramidal neurons in cortical regions.
source: The CaMKIIα promoter was used to enable transgene expression favoring pyramidal neurons (Liu and Jones, 1996 ) in cortical regions (Jones et al., 1994; Van den Oever et al., 2013; Warthen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on promoter specificity.

claim: PL projections to VS and BLA may target different neuronal populations within VS.
source: Activity in PL projections to VS decreases avoidance (top left projection). These projections may target fast-spiking interneurons within VS (orange neuron with question mark), which serve to inhibit VS output neurons.
evidence: Proposed model illustrated in Figure 4 with speculation about interneuron targeting.

claim: PL inputs to VS could gate the impact of BLA inputs on VS output neurons.
source: In this way, PL inputs to VS could gate the impact of BLA inputs on VS output neurons.
evidence: Proposed mechanism illustrated in Figure 4.
